content: Endometrial ablation is a medical procedure designed to remove or destroy the endometrial lining of the uterus. This treatment is primarily used for women who experience heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding and either cannot or do not wish to undergo a hysterectomy. The procedure is typically performed on an outpatient basis. However, it is not recommended for women who may wish to conceive in the future, as it significantly reduces the likelihood of successful pregnancy. There are several techniques available for performing endometrial ablation. Electrical energy is then applied to the mesh, which generates heat and destroys the adjacent endometrial tissue. Another approach uses a balloon that is filled with heated fluid to thermally ablate the uterine lining. Older techniques involve the use of hysteroscopy, where instruments are inserted into the uterus under direct visualization. These instruments may include lasers or small loops that deliver electrical currents to destroy the endometrial lining. A different system employs a radiofrequency rod that emits energy to ablate the uterine lining. The HTA (Hydrothermal Ablation) system is another option, which uses a hysteroscope—a small telescope-like device inserted through the cervix into the uterus—to allow the physician to visualize the treatment area. Heated saline is then circulated within the uterine cavity to destroy the endometrial lining. The procedure can be performed under local anesthesia, but in some cases, general or spinal anesthesia may be required. Recovery times vary, ranging from one day to up to two weeks. Following the procedure, the endometrial tissue heals through scarring, which significantly reduces or eliminates future uterine bleeding. Many patients develop amenorrhea (the absence of menstrual periods) after the procedure, but hormonal function remains unaffected. It is important to note that pregnancy is still possible after endometrial ablation, so patients must use a reliable form of contraception to prevent unintended pregnancies. The effectiveness of endometrial ablation is notable, with approximately 90% of women experiencing a reduction in menstrual bleeding. Among these, about 45% will stop having periods entirely. However, in approximately 22% of cases, a second procedure or a hysterectomy may be necessary to achieve the desired outcome. Although complications are rare, endometrial ablation carries some risks. These include perforation of the uterus, thermal injury extending beyond the endometrial lining, and, in very rare cases, pulmonary edema or embolism.
